newsitem.title: UK: News conference uproar after Saunders gagged.
newsitem.headline: News conference uproar after Saunders gagged.

text.p: A news conference given by former Guinness chairman Ernest Saunders on Tuesday ended in uproar after his "human rights consultant" George Devlin refused to allow Saunders to answer press questions.

Earlier, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Saunders had not received a fair trial in 1990 when he was found guilty of 12 counts including false accounting and theft for inflating the Guinness share price to help win a 1986 bid for Distillers Plc against a rival offer from Argyll Plc.
At the news conference, Saunders read a statement and answered a few questions but after this, despite the fact that questions were clearly directed at him, they received answers only from Devlin.
"My impression is that if the evidence had not been used I would have been acquitted," Saunders told reporters in his statement following news of the Strasbourg court's ruling.
"This is just the tip of the iceberg of a politically managed and totally unfair process. The government should not be allowed to manipulate the legal process for its own political agenda," he added.
Saunders said he would consider his options, confirmming that a further appeal to the English courts was one of them.
Two appeals have already been heard and rejected by England's Court of Appeal and a third will only be heard if the case is again referred by the British Home Secretary.
Saunders shrugged off a suggestion that he must be disappointed that his 4.6 million pounds ($7.66 million) claim for compensation from the European Court had been rejected.
"It's not a question of compensation, it's a matter of principle. That's sufficient," Saunders said.
From then on, Saunders remained quiet while Devlin fielded further questions.

At one point, it was put to Saunders that he was the only known person to have recovered from Alzheimer's disease which leads to premature senility and is always fatal, but Devlin said that the doctor who diagnosed Saunders as a sufferer has since publicly admitted that he made a mistake.
Saunders, now 61, was sentenced to five years for his part in the Guinness case which was later reduced to 2-1/2 years on appeal, but he was released after 10 months on the grounds of ill-health.

Amid complaints from journalists, one of whom pointed out that, for a human rights consultant, he seemed to be trying to gag his client, Devlin said: "If you don't like the way this press conference has been arranged, I suggest you leave."
After only 20 minutes and amid increasing anger from some journalists, Saunders turned to Devlin and suggested that the conference should end. ($1=.6003 Pound)
